name: Contouring injection surgery (fat removal)

card.summary: A family of Korean-style and clinic procedures, from fat-dissolving injections to buccal fat removal, that take volume out of the lower face to define cheeks, jawline and chin.
card.note: Fat removal is permanent; only one injectable (deoxycholic acid, for under-chin fat) is FDA-approved for fat reduction.

quick.overview:
Facial contouring by fat removal aims to slim the lower face so the cheekbones, jawline and chin read sharper. Options range from injections that dissolve fat, such as deoxycholic acid for the area under the chin, to minor surgery such as buccal fat removal, where a small pad of fat is taken from each cheek.

Filler studies often sit in the same clinics: separate trials test hyaluronic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite fillers for jawline contour, which add volume rather than remove it. Evidence for fat-dissolving injections is mostly retrospective; one product has regulatory approval for the chin area.
quick.how: In clinics, a practitioner marks the area and either injects a fat-dissolving drug over several sessions or, for buccal fat removal, removes fat through a small incision inside the mouth, usually under local anesthesia in about 30 minutes. Swelling settles over days and final results may take up to three months.
quick.risks: Buccal fat removal can injure facial nerve branches or the parotid duct, and the loss is permanent, so cheeks may look hollow with age. Unapproved fat-dissolving mixtures have drawn FDA warning letters, and reports describe scarring, deformation and painful lumps. Kybella commonly causes swelling, bruising and numbness.

lead: Contouring by fat removal covers procedures meant to slim parts of the lower face. Practitioners and patients, including many in the Korean aesthetics market, use injections that destroy fat cells or small surgeries that remove fat to sharpen the jawline, chin and cheek hollows.[1]

Two procedures dominate. Injection lipolysis uses drug mixtures, usually phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate, in many small injections over several sessions to destroy fat cells.[3] Buccal fat removal takes a small portion of the buccal fat pad from each cheek through an intraoral incision to reduce cheek fullness.[4] The only fat-reducing injectable approved by the FDA is deoxycholic acid (Kybella), approved April 29, 2015 for moderate-to-severe fat below the chin.[5]
On looksmax.org, buccal fat removal is a recurring subject, with threads on results, hesitation, regret, consensus and do-it-yourself attempts.[6][7][8]

chain: Remove or dissolve fat in cheeks or under the chin

angle.text: These procedures reduce fat that obscures bone and muscle contours. People choose them for a slimmer, more angular lower face when diet alone does not change facial fullness.

paras: Injection lipolysis mixes drugs, often phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate, which are injected under the skin in many small doses across multiple sessions to destroy fat cells.[3] Deoxycholic acid injected into submental fat breaks down fat cells, which the body clears over several months.[5]

Buccal fat removal is a cosmetic surgery removing a small piece of the buccal fat pad from each cheek, typically under local anesthesia through an incision near the upper second molar, taking about 30 minutes; it generally has no medical benefit, so insurance seldom covers it.[4]

The buccal fat pad was described by Lorenz Heister in 1732 as glandular tissue and identified as fat by Xavier Bichat in 1802.[4] Interest rose after Chrissy Teigen revealed in 2021 that she had the procedure, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons counted 4,543 procedures in 2022, its first year tracking it.[4]

Injection lipolysis traces to intravenous phosphatidylcholine, with German formulations such as Lipostabil used for decades and studies by Rotunda and colleagues in 2005 and 2006.[3] In 2015 the FDA approved deoxycholic acid for double chin.[3][5]

Buccal fat removal risks include injury to the buccal branch of the facial nerve (possible numbness, partial paralysis or loss of taste) and to the parotid duct (saliva collections). The removal is permanent, and the article notes that removing the fat may make a person look gaunt as cheeks lose volume with age.[4]

In 2010 the FDA sent warning letters to U.S. medspas and a Brazilian company over 'lipodissolve' claims, stating the products were not approved for fat removal; Kybella is the only approved product, and only for submental fullness.[3] The article reports no placebo-controlled studies showing the mixtures are safe or effective and FDA reports of scarring, deformation and painful knots.[3]

Forum threads include success stories ('saved my mental health'), questions about whether a 24-year-old with chubby cheeks should do it, requests for tips, and discussions on whether removal replaces getting lean.[9][10][11] A thread titled as a 'perfect hardmaxx or the worst mistake' reflects the split in opinion about it.[12]

A 2017 Radiographics review covered soft-tissue procedures in plastic surgery, including contouring by liposuction, fat grafting and injections, from the perspective of how they appear on imaging.[1] Registered filler trials on jawline contour, for example Radiesse in 180 participants (NCT03583359) and a trial of LANLUMA V in 192 participants, test volume addition rather than fat removal.[13][14]

timeline.event: Lorenz Heister describes the buccal fat pad.[4]
Xavier Bichat identifies it as fat.[4]
FDA warning letters over lipodissolve claims.[3]
FDA approves deoxycholic acid (Kybella) for under-chin fat.[5]
Chrissy Teigen discloses buccal fat removal; interest rises.[4]
ASPS begins tracking buccal fat removal, recording 4,543 procedures.[4]
